title: Steady States of a Single Trapped-Ion Spin Coupled to an Engineered Non-Markovian Bath
authors: Anthony Vogliano, Lewis Hahn, Fabien Lefebvre, Jingwen Zhu, Sakshee Patil, Mahmood Sabooni, Zhexuan Gong, Rajibul Islam
abstract: Quantum simulation of open quantum systems offers a pathway towards better understanding various non-equilibrium physics that would otherwise be challenging to study. Most open quantum systems studied are modeled as obeying the Markov approximation, where the bath into which the system dissipates information is assumed to be unaffected by the system-bath interaction. However, real baths are in general influenced by this interaction to some degree, and some systems which exist in structured non-Markovian environments can display novel behavior as a result. Here we utilize a trapped ion quantum simulator to simulate a single spin-$1/2$ driven-dissipative system with a non-Markovian dissipation channel, and experimentally compare steady-states to those from an analogous Markovian bath. We observe that a non-Markovian dissipative channel can dramatically change the steady-state even for a single qubit, to a regime inaccessible for Markovian dissipation. This demonstrates the added richness available to quantum systems in structured environments. The techniques used here are compatible with many-body extensions of the model, which can not be simulated efficiently on a classical computer in general. Our work also opens up new possibilities in quantum reservoir engineering beyond the Markovian regime.
summary: The paper investigates how engineered non-Markovian dissipation affects the steady state of a single trapped ion spin. By simulating these complex dynamics using trapped ions, the authors experimentally demonstrate that memory effects in the bath can fundamentally change the system's final equilibrium state compared to simpler Markovian models. This opens new avenues for quantum reservoir engineering beyond standard approximations.
main_problem: The study aims to understand non-equilibrium physics in open quantum systems where the environment (bath) is structured, leading to non-Markovian memory effects.
main_result: Non-Markovian dissipation can dramatically alter the steady-state of a single qubit compared to Markovian models, allowing access to novel dissipative regimes inaccessible otherwise.
method: The authors simulate the system using trapped ion quantum simulators by implementing engineered non-Markovian bath profiles via probabilistic reset sequences approximating ensemble averages over quantum trajectories.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a single spin-1/2 trapped $^{171}	ext{Yb}^+$ ion. The dynamics are modeled using generalized master equations, contrasting the standard Lindblad (Markovian) form with memory kernel approaches for non-Markovian baths.
key_observables: Steady-state magnetization ($\langle M_x angle, \langle M_z angle$) of the spin system.
important_parameters: The ratio of effective dissipation rate to coherent drive strength ($\Gamma_{	ext{eff}}/B$), and the correlation structure parameter $\alpha$ (e.g., for a Pareto-correlated bath).
main_assumptions: The simulation relies on approximating the ensemble average over quantum trajectories using deterministic reset profiles, which is compatible with many-body extensions.
figures_summary: Figures compare expected vs. experimental steady-state magnetization, showing that non-Markovianity allows for a positive magnetization in the $-	ext{z}$ direction, contrary to Markovian predictions.
paper_structure: The work establishes the theoretical framework using generalized master equations, details the trapped ion implementation via engineered reset profiles, and presents comparative results demonstrating the unique steady-state signatures of non-Markovian coupling.
why_interesting: This is highly relevant as it pushes beyond standard Markovian approximations in open quantum systems, providing experimental evidence for novel physics arising from structured environments, which is a frontier area in quantum optics and AMO physics.
